newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Smallest UK PSBR for six years.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Smallest UK PSBR for six years.

text.p: When Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown stands up to present his first budget on July 2, he will be able to predict the smallest public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) for six years, a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.

The survey, carried out between June 19 and 20, suggested there is little likelihood of swingeing increases in taxation and that Brown will unveil a relatively modest tightening of just four billion sterling, to help take the heat out of the feverish economy.

The median of 20 forecasts from British economists is for a 1997-98 PSBR of just 16.0 billion stg, down from just under 23 billion in 1996-97. By 1998-99, there is even better news with the deficit poised to tumble to just 12.0 billion, the survey says.

The forecast of the smallest net rise in taxes was just 1.5 billion stg from First Chicago economist Stewart Newnham, who is amongst the minority of economists surveyed who does not expect a change to Advance Corporation Tax (ACT). The highest forecast -- from a firm which declined to be named -- was eight billion sterling, based on the expectation that ACT would be scrapped altogether, raising some five billion sterling.

Analysts said the overall state of public finances is not perfect -- the UK has a structural budget deficit of some three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- inconsistent with Labour's "golden rule" of only borrowing to fund investment.
And Brown would also need to tighten policy if he were aiming to hit the ousted Conservative Party's target of a balanced budget over the economic cycle.
"Ironically the only basis on which the UK doesn't need to tighten fiscal policy is if it wants to go into the (European) single currency," said Co-operative Bank UK economist Andrew Snowball.

The Maastricht convergence criteria state that the public sector deficit should not exceed three percent of GDP in 1997. European economic and monetary union is timetabled to start on January 1, 1999.

Snowball expected Brown to predict a PSBR of around 17.0 billion sterling for fiscal 1997-98, down from former Conservative Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's prediction of a 19.2 billion deficit. Snowball expects the deficit to move down to 14.0 billion next year.

If Brown wanted to do something about the size of the UK's structural deficit, then the present momemt, just two months after the Labour party's landslide election victory, would be the perfect time, according to IBJ chief economist Stephen Hannah. "They should be tightening by somewhere between five and 10 billion sterling and now is an ideal time to do it," he said. "But the political reality is that a five billion figure is much closer to what is likely to emerge."
Labour has fought hard to shake off its image as a high tax, high spending party and, after 18 years in opposition, it is unlikely to risk alienating voters with its first budget.

"It will go for soft targets," said Business Strategies senior economist Andrew Schofield. He expects the budget to raise about four billion sterling through reducing ACT to 10 percent from its current level of 20 percent and by axeing tax relief on MIRAS (mortgage interest relief at source.)

"If you've got to raise money from somewhere, MIRAS will cause less of a squeal this year," he said, arguing that many mortgage holders have received a hefty inflow of cash from building society mergers and flotations.

Analysts warn that if, as most of those surveyed suggested, the majority of tax increases were targeted at the corporate and not the buoyant consumer sector, then interest rates would have to take the strain in terms of preventing the economy from overheating.
"The big issue is still what the balance between monetary and fiscal policy is going to be and my suspicion is that we are moving towards a more aggressive monetary stance," IBJ's Hannah said.
Brown raised official interest rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent in May and then ceded control of monetary policy to the Bank of England.

With an eye on the inflation horizon two years ahead, the central bank raised interest rates to 6.5 percent in June and Hannah predicts they will reach 7.0 by the end of the year, as interest rates are used as the main tool of demand management.
